y4-ht2.summary: Our own unit, 6 lessons, with Marie and Pierre. Verbs (infinitives): danser, chanter, sauter, cuisiner, faire du vélo, jouer au foot, patiner, dessiner, nager, parler français; extension (all -er): jouer d'un instrument, jouer de la guitare, jouer au hockey, grimper, skier. page.intro: How the French scheme for Years 3 and 4 is built: what we want pupils to achieve, how every lesson works, the activities we use, and how learning builds over two years.
intent: French is fun and engaging, and built on evidence of what makes language learning stick, not only what makes it enjoyable.

Pupils grow the confidence to listen, speak and hold real conversations. The audience grows on purpose: a partner, a small group, the class, then parents or an assembly, older pupils, and finally a new teacher.
A planned cultural strand with several touchpoints each year, tied to units and the calendar, not left to chance.
A have-a-go culture, supported by quick checks every lesson, so pupils and teachers know where they stand long before any test.
page.pillars: Phonics, vocabulary and grammar are taught as three explicit, interwoven strands. Phonics and retrieval always come before new language.
lesson: Read known and new words with the sound of the half term aloud (decoding).
Hear it, write it: the same sounds the other way round (encoding).
Picture → say the French. Spaced and mixed so pupils know more and remember more.
New language one item at a time, big in the middle, then all together (Tous ensemble).
Guided practice: games, songs, paired talk and worked examples.
Independent work: write first, then draw. Assessment evidence is gathered here.
How did it go? What's next? (« Où est Pierre ? » and optional games for spare time.)
research: The National Curriculum for languages (Key Stage 2)
The statutory programme of study: listening, speaking, reading, writing and grammar. Every unit is assessed against its codes.
NCELP (National Centre for Excellence for Language Pedagogy)
Teaching sound, vocabulary and grammar systematically, and revisiting earlier language through spaced retrieval.
SEND Code of Practice (2015) and EEF guidance on SEN in mainstream schools
Behind the Inclusion work: high-quality teaching for every pupil, adapted so that all pupils can take part in the same lesson.
Cognitive load theory (routines and small steps so children are not overwhelmed), dual coding (the French word paired with its picture) and the SOLO taxonomy of Biggs and Collis, used for assessment.
Phonics, vocabulary and grammar as the three pillars of progress.
Daily review, new material in small steps, guided then independent practice.
Retrieval practice, spacing and interleaving to reduce cognitive load.

Sue Cave’s primary phonics guidance informs the practical phonics activity bank, including Pause and Say, Phonic Bingo, Phonic Happy Families and Find Your Group. The scheme’s Fire and Hire routine is an adapted classroom variation.
vocabulary: A small, useful core set (anchored to the words pupils will need later at GCSE). Every pupil is taught and assessed on it.

Each pupil has a dedicated mes mots section to add additional French vocabulary linked to their own interests. This sits alongside the shared core vocabulary and gives pupils ownership of extending their language. It also helps keep every pupil interested.

Pupils can add notes, reminders and examples, highlight the digraphs being studied, mark silent letters, and use their own colours or symbols to notice sound, spelling patterns. Teachers model useful annotation. Pupils are encouraged to retrieve language from memory and use the mat selectively as their independence grows.

Core words are chosen because pupils can use them straight away to talk about themselves (name, age, feelings, likes, what they can do). We favour high-frequency words and verbs that come back in later units, so pupils keep using them, and words that contain the sounds being taught, so phonics and vocabulary support each other. Topic words are kept to a small, useful set.

phonics: Teacher shows a word; pause; everyone says it together.
Bingo boards of sound words; listen and cover.
Collect words that share the same sound.
Pupils hold word cards and find others with the same sound.
lesson: In this classroom variation, point at a picture on the board and say a word. If it matches, the class repeats it; if it does not, pupils stay silent. Sometimes a child leads at the board. This is the scheme’s adapted routine, not a claim that it is identical to every published version of Fire and Hire.

Two real toys with their own personalities, who only speak French. Marie (a teddy) is shy, timid, calm and quiet. Her best friend Pierre (a toy duck) is loud, cheeky and outgoing. Hold one up and pupils speak or sing to match: quiet for Marie, loud for Pierre, especially during songs. Pupils talk to them and ask them questions in French. A child who is upset or feeling down can keep Marie or Pierre at their table. Pierre also hides for the game « Où est Pierre ? », which pupils love.
Ask yes/no questions to find a hidden character: on the board first, then in pairs.
Two pupils race to splat the picture of the word they hear.
Picture or word boards; the caller says the French and pupils cover it.
Learn the unit song, then fill in missing words in the lyrics.
One picture disappears; pupils say which one has gone.
Pupils make the cards, then say the French every time they turn one.
Roll for a picture (and a colour); say the full sentence.
Sort words or pictures into groups, then explain the choice.
Answer the question, say « Et toi ? » and throw the ball to someone new.
Ask friends a question and record the answers; look at the results together.
Find your partner's ships by saying grid words in French.
Short dialogues with puppets or in role (café, interview…).
Retrieval games to recall vocabulary quickly.
assess: The end-of-unit review (Lesson 6), done with nothing on display, in Class, Adapted and Inclusion versions. Pupils show and reflect on what they can do. In HT2, HT4 and HT6 it also gives written evidence for the formal checkpoint codes; in HT1, HT3 and HT5 it is formative.
Speaking and listening codes are judged during planned activities: the survey, Guess Who?, songs, conversations and performances.
The teacher listens to pairs and notes speaking and listening evidence.
Pupils rate themselves on the What I can do sheet.
Reading aloud and transcription checks, three times across the two years.
Instant checks every lesson to adapt teaching straight away.

phonics.note: From Year 3, every time new vocabulary is written, pupils look for the sounds they know and the silent letters. About three sound words and one or two traps per lesson. Do not create separate tricky-word lists: those words are learnt by heart. The phonics apps bring back sounds from earlier half-terms so pupils revisit previously taught patterns.

grammar.y3: Chunks (HT1 to 2) → un / une with je suis (HT3) → the colour after the noun (HT3 to 4) → je vois / tu vois (HT4) → opinions joined with et / mais (HT5). No adjective agreement.
grammar.y4: Je peux / tu peux + infinitive and ne … pas (HT2) → j'ai + noun, with qui s'appelle and je n'ai pas de as chunks (HT3) → partitive and past tense heard, not produced (HT4) → polite vous (HT5) → il / elle understood (HT6).

page.audience: Partner → small group → whole class → parents or assembly (Le Zoo Rigolo !) → older pupils (Le Café Français) → a new teacher (Tout sur moi, handed on at the end of Year 4).
page.books: Two picture books anchor the two years, both in Spring 2 (HT4): Ours brun, ours brun, que vois-tu ? in Year 3 (short and repetitive) and La Chenille qui fait des trous in Year 4 (a step up, with the past tense heard). The same half term also holds a phonics progress check.

y3: Bienvenue au monde francophone: countries where French is spoken, and how people greet each other in France, Belgium and Québec (la bise, a handshake)
Noël: le réveillon, la bûche de Noël, les marchés de Noël, le calendrier de l'Avent
What animals say in French (ouaf ouaf, miaou, coin-coin), and animals you might see in other French-speaking countries (a moose in Québec, a lion in Senegal)
Ours brun, an authentic picture book; Easter: les cloches, chocolate fish and le poisson d'avril
French sport, sportspeople from different French-speaking countries, and Wednesday afternoons: many French primary pupils have no school, so it is time for clubs and sport
Birthdays: « Joyeux anniversaire », the birthday song, French birthday cards, and le goûter, the after-school snack in France and Belgium
y4: Le monde francophone revisited; la rentrée and the French school day
Christmas in French-speaking countries: Saint-Nicolas in Belgium, le réveillon in Québec, the fanal lanterns in Senegal
Geography and landmarks: the Eiffel Tower, French regions and cities, a couple of fun facts about two other French-speaking countries, and la cantine: lunch at a French school
La Chenille qui fait des trous, an authentic picture book
Café culture: ordering politely, with older pupils as visitors
La Fête nationale (14 juillet), a glimpse of Québec's own fête nationale (24 June), and les grandes vacances: the long summer holiday

inclusion: The fixed core only, more scaffolding held for longer, more repetition and spaced retrieval, fewer choices at once. Use the Adapted sheets.

Individual support, with no single template: resources follow the child's interests and needs, with manipulatives and picture support. Pupils may step back from fast spontaneous games such as Guess Who. Use the Inclusion sheets and simple word mats.

Ofsted's languages research review (2021) found that the proportion of boys, disadvantaged pupils and pupils with SEND who carry on with languages after Key Stage 3 is low. So engagement is planned from Year 3, for every pupil: games and songs, Marie and Pierre, a real purpose and a growing audience, and personal choice through the mes mots section of the word mat, where pupils add French linked to their own interests. Teachers notice who is losing interest and respond to each pupil's actual needs.
An extension vocabulary bank, and challenge provided within the Class work.

These pupils usually speak and understand French well, so their focus is on reading and writing. Where it suits the pupil, they are also offered a second language, currently Spanish, to push their curiosity.
assessment: Each of the 12 assessment codes receives one formal SOLO judgement per academic year, at the planned checkpoint. Other unit activities and day-to-day checks provide formative evidence and inform teaching; they do not create additional annual judgements.

Formal judgements use task-specific descriptors at SOLO 3 (multistructural), SOLO 4 (relational) or SOLO 5 (extended abstract). A pupil not yet at SOLO 3 is assessed as SOLO 2 (unistructural) or SOLO 1 (prestructural). Do not use a generic level description in place of the descriptor for the actual task.

The pupil-facing end-of-unit review, normally in Lesson 6, gives pupils an opportunity to reflect using I’ve got it, Nearly there and Not yet. Self-assessment is valuable but is not the teacher’s formal SOLO judgement.

Reading, writing and grammar evidence comes from the task matched to the objective. When recall from memory is assessed, prompts must not give away the answer; when using a word list or word mat is the skill being assessed, that resource should be available.

Speaking and listening are assessed through planned interactions, conversations, games and performances. The teacher records each pupil’s own contribution; a partner’s response or success is not a substitute for the pupil’s evidence.

During book work, note observable evidence: recognising familiar language, following events, joining in with repeated phrases, anticipating familiar patterns, making connections and responding to characters or events. Responses may be spoken, gestural, by pointing, choosing or sequencing. Do not assess personality or outward enthusiasm.

L2 connects spelling, sound and meaning. S3 assesses accurate sound production and pronunciation. They are related but distinct; pronunciation evidence gathered during phonics practice can also be formative S3 evidence.
Teacher circulation, mini-whiteboards, hands and thumbs, retrieval and phonics practice help teachers respond during lessons. These checks are not extra formal SOLO judgements.
Use the formal checkpoint evidence to review how many pupils are below SOLO 4, at SOLO 4 and at SOLO 5 for each code, alongside the quality of the work and any support used.
impact: Compare each pupil’s evidence for the same assessment code across Year 3 and Year 4. Consider the task demands and independence shown, not just the numerical SOLO level.

Use the three common reading-aloud and transcription progress checks to review development across the two-year sequence. Record the level of scaffold used; raw scores alone are not a fair comparison when scaffolding changes.
Review dated work over time, including Mon bilan, the Ours brun book, birthday cards and the Tout sur moi profile. Look for retrieval, increasing accuracy and independent application.
Use What I can do reflections and pupils’ mes mots choices. Ask pupils what they are learning, which strategies help them remember French and what they can now do independently.
Tout sur moi is handed on to the next teacher at the end of Year 4 as a tangible example of each pupil’s language learning.
Keep exemplar work and assessment evidence from each term. Revisit a sample of SOLO judgements against task-specific descriptors so expectations are understood consistently.
Use patterns in assessment, work scrutiny and pupil voice to decide what to revisit, reteach or adapt. Review tasks that do not provide valid evidence for their intended objective.

directAssociation: Use pictures, objects, actions and meaningful contexts so pupils connect the concept directly with the French word. For example, show an apple, say une pomme, and use it in context. English is not an obligatory intermediate step.

Make explicit comparisons when they help pupils understand how languages work: sounds, spelling, word order, nouns, determiners, adjectives, verbs and sentence structures. English is a useful point of comparison, not the default route for introducing French vocabulary.

Listening, speaking, reading and writing are all developed. Writing is a core skill, not an afterthought to oracy. Pupils decode written French, connect it directly with meaning, write from memory and adapt familiar structures.

Audio should be embedded in teaching slides wherever French words, questions or answers are presented. This supports accurate pronunciation and helps non-specialist teachers model and revisit spoken French.
Mistakes are a normal part of learning. Anticipate likely misconceptions, model clearly, use small steps and guided practice, and check understanding frequently so that teaching can respond.
pupilResources: A pupil-facing record of progressive learning statements, built across the unit. For example, pupils may first learn five colours, then five more, and then use them to ask and answer questions. Pupils reflect using I’ve got it, Nearly there and Not yet.
The What I can do sheet records the half-term sound focus. The cultural learning for that unit appears directly underneath the sound focus, so both are visible within the same pupil learning journey.
The sheet includes space for the relevant assessment codes, the formal SOLO judgement and teacher notes. Pupil reflection and teacher assessment are connected but are not the same thing.
The word mat grows lesson by lesson. It contains the shared core vocabulary, useful phrases and sentence structures pupils have learnt so far; it is not a static translation list.

Each pupil adds extra French vocabulary connected to their own interests in the mes mots section. They can also add notes, reminders and examples, highlight the digraphs being studied, mark silent letters and use their own colours or symbols to notice patterns.
Teachers model how to use and annotate the mat. Pupils use it to retrieve, select and combine language, then increasingly rely on memory and consult the mat selectively as their independence grows.

think: Why does every lesson start with phonics?
It is a warm-up that prepares pupils for the lesson ahead. Through continuous practice they can decode more and more words, they grow in confidence, and their pronunciation improves.
Why is retrieval always at the beginning?
To make connections with prior learning before anything new is introduced.
Why does every lesson follow the same shape?

Routines help children feel safe and stop them feeling overwhelmed. The slides are clear and show what is expected, so every child knows what they are doing at all times. Because the routine takes care of itself, children can concentrate on the new content.
Why do pupils see the picture before the word?
To avoid misconceptions and the bad habits that come from reading a word incorrectly. We also avoid learning French word, then English word, then image. We go from the French word to the image.
Why is grammar explained?
So children understand what they are doing, rather than only copying a pattern.
Why colour coding?
It helps children understand how a sentence works, and remember it.
Why are the worksheets laid out so clearly?

To avoid cognitive overload, not to make the work easy. Often the sheet is just a picture to prompt the writing, so pupils focus on the French rather than deciding what to write. One clear task, a calm layout, picture prompts and the question at the top mean pupils put their effort into the French, not into working out what to do. The challenge is in the language.
Why write first and draw afterwards?
Pupils do the hard work first and then draw, so that more of their time is spent thinking about the new content.
Why does writing matter?

Written tasks are not only there for the writing objectives. When pupils write, they have to retrieve the words, notice the sounds and spellings, and put the grammar into practice. Writing gives pupils the time to stop, reflect and consolidate what they have learnt, which helps them remember the language and use it more securely. It is part of how pupils learn French, not just a final outcome.
What makes a good game?

Children use the language they know and meet no barriers, because the game is easy to follow. Games are normally played in pairs or teams, while the teacher walks around, observes and gives feedback. We avoid games where children get out of control or need to shout.
Why does the audience grow?
There is a progression from small and comfortable to wider and more challenging. Pupils get motivated and see a purpose for what they are preparing, so the learning is meaningful.
Why are there different levels of work?

We think of all our pupils. Most work at Class level. Adapted is the same work with scaffolding. Challenge is provided within the Class work. Inclusion is for those who cannot access what the rest of the class is doing, and they still feel part of the group because their work links to each day's objective.
Why is there cut and stick and joining in the Inclusion work?

Inclusion work is adapted to the individual pupil: the task, presentation, scaffolding and resources change, while the learning stays meaningful and linked to the day's objective. Practical formats such as cut and stick and joining often work well, because they reduce the writing load and let pupils talk about their learning with support staff as they work. They are chosen for each pupil, not assumed for all pupils with special educational needs (SEN).
Why SOLO?
SOLO shows how deep a pupil's understanding is, not just how many answers are right. It moves from knowing separate words, to linking them into sentences, to using language in new ways.
Why Mon bilan?

It is structured and can be done under controlled conditions. Pupils show and reflect on what they can do, and in HT2, HT4 and HT6 it gives clear written evidence for the formal checkpoint. Speaking and listening are observed during planned activities.
marie: Two real toys with their own personalities. Marie, a teddy, is shy, timid, calm and quiet. Her best friend Pierre, a toy duck, is loud, cheeky and outgoing.
They began as a class mascot. It went so well that they were given personalities. Children ask about them when the teacher arrives, or if they have not been brought out.

When Marie is held up, the class sings quietly. When Pierre is held up, they sing loudly. Everyone joins in, even children who show challenging behaviour. It also helps to keep the class quiet at the end of a song, ready to listen.
So children have to use their knowledge of French to speak to them. Pupils talk to them and ask them questions.
A child who is upset or feeling down can keep Marie or Pierre at their table.
Pierre hides for this hide-and-seek game, and the class says the word louder as the seeker gets closer. Children love it.

progressShows: Every half term adds new vocabulary and a new grammar step, so the same code is assessed on harder French: chunks, un / une and colours in Year 3; je peux + infinitive, ne … pas, j'ai and vous in Year 4.
More at the same SOLO level
Each checkpoint task has its own SOLO descriptors. SOLO 4 in Year 4 asks for longer, linked sentences and more independence than SOLO 4 in Year 3 (see the end-of-year statements below).
Scaffolds are reduced over time. In phonics, transcription moves from a choice of 2 in Year 3 to free transcription in Year 4.
Pupils speak and write for a partner, then a group, the class, parents, older pupils and finally a new teacher.
Each code is judged once a year, so a pupil's SOLO level for the same code can be compared across both years.

handbook.believe: Children learn a language when they are engaged and see a purpose for it. They use it in real scenarios and it covers their interests. Playing games allows repetition and engagement. We want them to be as involved as possible, using all they have learnt as they keep learning.
